title: Table saw: get the motor, arbor and cast-iron top
summary: A table saw gives you a strong 1.5-5 hp induction motor (or a 1.5-2 kW universal motor on a jobsite saw), a precision arbor with bearings, V-belts and pulleys, steel rails, worm gears, a magnetic starter and a flat cast-iron top. Allow about an hour and a helper for the heavy parts. Unplug it first: the blade is sharp even when it is still.

steps.text: Pull the plug out of the wall and put it where you can see it. A hard-wired saw: switch off and tag its breaker and prove the wires dead (see safety_mains_isolation). Don't trust the switch or a stopped blade.
steps.warn: A saw that starts while your hand is near the blade can take fingers in a fraction of a second. Keep the plug in your hand or in sight.

steps.text: Take off the blade guard, the riving knife (the thin steel plate behind the blade) and the throat plate (the insert around the blade). Raise the blade as high as it goes. Put on thick gloves.

Take the blade off. Hold the teeth with a thick rag and put one wrench on the arbor flats and another on the nut. Check which way the nut turns before you force it: on many saws it is left-hand thread (clockwise to loosen), on others right-hand; look for an arrow or an LH mark, or try a gentle turn each way. Take the nut, flange and blade off together. Wrap the blade in cardboard and tape it up.
steps.warn: The blade is sharp even when it has stopped. Never hold it by bare teeth and never let a wrench slip towards it.

steps.text: Take the fence, the fence rails and the miter gauge: unbolt the rails at the front and back (usually two or three bolts each side). Keep the bolts with their rails.

Photograph the wiring, then take out the magnetic starter or switch box with its wiring (or cut the cord 20 cm from the switch). Unscrew the motor's junction box cover and label each wire before you unplug anything.
Discharge the motor's start or run capacitor (a cylinder on or beside the motor) with the resistor tool from safety_discharge_capacitor, then measure it before you touch its terminals.
steps.warn: A motor capacitor can hold a charge for days. Don't touch its terminals until it reads near zero.

steps.text: Support the motor and take it off. Loosen its mounting bolts and the belt tension, slip the V-belts off, then lift. A 1.5-3 hp induction motor weighs 15-25 kg: use two people. Keep the pulley, its key and set screw on the shaft. Jobsite saws have a smaller universal motor bolted to the arbor housing: undo it as one unit.
steps.warn: A 20 kg motor dropped on a foot breaks bones. Use a helper or a block and tackle.

steps.text: Take the arbor assembly: the shaft with its bearings and housing, still attached to its carrier or trunnion. Undo the bolts that hold it to the saw, noting how they sit. Keep the bearings in the housing; pull them only with a puller or a press.
Take the raise and tilt gearing: handwheels, threaded rods and worm gears. Mark the position of each gear before you take it off so it can go back the same way.

Take the cast-iron top last. First take off the wings (bolts along the sides), then the top: undo the bolts at the corners while a helper holds it. A cast-iron top with wings is 30-80 kg. Lay it flat on blocks, not on the ground. Jobsite saws have a lighter aluminium or steel top.
steps.warn: Cast iron is brittle and heavy. A dropped top can break and crush a foot. Lift with two people (see safety_lifting).

steps.text: Test the motor before you carry it far: spin the shaft by hand (smooth, no grinding), and check the windings and the insulation to the frame with your meter (see test_motor).

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Induction motor.** The prize: quiet, long-lived and strong, 1.5-5 hp (1.1-3.7 kW). Drives a lathe, a grain mill, a water pump, a compressor or a grinder. Read its plate (see skill_read_nameplate): many are dual-voltage and can be rewired. As a generator, an induction motor needs capacitors and a prime mover; see capacitor_large.
- **Universal motor.** 1.5-2 kW, 10,000+ rpm, runs on AC or DC. Loud and short-lived but very powerful for its size. Replace worn brushes with repair_motor_brushes.
- **Arbor with bearings.** A ready-made spindle: a grinding wheel, a buffer, a sanding disc or a small circular saw.
- **Cast-iron top.** Flat, heavy and stable: a workbench top, an anvil base, a surface plate for checking flat parts, a welding table.
- **Fence and rails.** Straight steel tube and an aluminium fence: a straightedge, a guide rail, a bench frame.
- **V-belts and pulleys.** Match pulleys to the motor to change speed.
- **Worm gears and threaded rods.** For a lift or a tilting stand.
- **Magnetic starter.** A relay with overload protection: a safe switch for any motor of similar rating.
- **Blade.** A carbide blade is brittle. Keep it wrapped; it makes a good saw blade for a circular saw of the same size.

## Before you strip it

- A sound table saw makes planks and furniture; a workshop may need it more than your parts bin does. Check whether it runs before you strip it, with the blade off and everyone clear of the blade path.
- Bandsaws, drill presses and jointers in the same workshops use the same kind of induction motor.

## What to leave

- The plastic guard if cracked, a bent fence, a rusty blade with missing teeth.
- A saw with a flesh-sensing brake (SawStop type): leave the brake cartridge in place and don't touch its sensing wiring.
